q: Under the first method of lending recommended by the Tandon Committee, the maximum permissible bank finance is 75 per cent of the working capital gap, that is, current assets minus current liabilities other than bank borrowings. An enterprise has current assets of Rs 36,00,000 and such other current liabilities of Rs 12,00,000. Its maximum permissible bank finance under this method is:
e: Working capital gap = Rs 36,00,000 - Rs 12,00,000 = Rs 24,00,000. Maximum permissible bank finance under Tandon Method I = 75% of Rs 24,00,000 = Rs 18,00,000.

q: The Chore Committee on the cash credit system recommended, among other things, that:

options.A: The borrower should be given a single undifferentiated cash credit limit for the whole year, with no review of its utilisation
options.B: Separate limits should be fixed for the peak season and the non-peak (normal) season, and the borrower should furnish quarterly statements of expected receipts and payments against the sanctioned limits
options.C: Banks should stop taking stock statements from borrowers enjoying working capital limits
options.D: The entire working capital requirement of a borrower should be met from long-term sources only

e: The Chore Committee recommended separate peak-season and non-peak limits, with quarterly statements of expected receipts and payments, to discipline cash credit use.

q: Working capital is estimated by the projected balance sheet method by:

options.A: Taking a fixed percentage of the projected sales of the coming year, without preparing any statement
options.B: Dividing the annual operating cost by the number of operating cycles in the year
options.C: Applying the current ratio of the previous year to the previous year's current liabilities
options.D: Preparing a forecast balance sheet for a future date, in which the projected current assets minus the projected current liabilities (other than the bank borrowing to be ascertained) give the working capital gap to be financed

e: The projected balance sheet method forecasts current assets and liabilities; projected CA minus projected CL other than bank borrowing gives the working capital gap to finance.

q: An enterprise has permanent current assets of Rs 15,00,000 throughout the year and temporary current assets rising to Rs 6,00,000 at the seasonal peak. Following the matching (hedging) approach strictly, it should finance:

options.A: The whole Rs 21,00,000 from short-term sources, renewing them as they fall due
options.B: The permanent current assets of Rs 15,00,000 from long-term sources and the temporary current assets of Rs 6,00,000 from short-term sources
options.C: The whole Rs 21,00,000 from long-term sources, keeping the seasonal part idle in the slack season
options.D: The permanent current assets from short-term sources and the temporary current assets from long-term sources

e: Under the matching approach, permanent current assets are financed from long-term sources and temporary seasonal assets from short-term sources, matching maturity to need.

q: Compared with an aggressive working capital financing policy, a conservative policy generally results in:

options.A: Lower liquidity and higher profitability, because long-term funds are costlier and are used sparingly
options.B: Higher risk of being unable to renew short-term borrowings on maturity
options.C: Higher liquidity and lower profitability, because costlier long-term funds are used even for seasonal needs and surplus funds remain idle in the slack season
options.D: No difference at all in either liquidity or profitability

e: A conservative policy uses costlier long-term funds even for seasonal needs, leaving surplus idle in slack periods, so liquidity is higher but profitability is lower.

q: In estimating the working capital of a manufacturing enterprise, debtors are commonly valued at the cost of sales rather than at the selling price, because:

options.A: The profit element in the selling price is not a fund actually blocked in the debtors; only the cost incurred has to be financed until collection
options.B: The selling price of the goods is never known in advance
options.C: Debtors are not a current asset at all
options.D: Credit sales are always made at a loss

e: Only cost is actually blocked in debtors; the profit element in selling price is not an outlay needing finance, so debtors are valued at cost of sales.

q: A factory has 10,000 units in work-in-progress. Material costing Rs 40 per unit has been fully introduced, while labour of Rs 20 per unit and overheads of Rs 10 per unit (at full completion) are only 50 per cent complete on these units. The value of the work-in-progress to be taken in the working capital estimate is:
e: WIP value = material Rs 40 x 10,000 + labour Rs 20 x 50% x 10,000 + overhead Rs 10 x 50% x 10,000 = Rs 4,00,000 + Rs 1,00,000 + Rs 50,000 = Rs 5,50,000.

q: The annual demand for a material is 18,000 units, its Economic Order Quantity is 600 units, the ordering cost is Rs 50 per order and the carrying cost is Rs 5 per unit per year. At the Economic Order Quantity, the total annual ordering cost plus carrying cost is:
e: Orders = 18,000 / 600 = 30, ordering cost = 30 x Rs 50 = Rs 1,500. Carrying cost = (600/2) x Rs 5 = Rs 1,500. Total = Rs 3,000, the two being equal at EOQ.

q: The annual demand for a component is 24,000 units and its Economic Order Quantity is 800 units. The number of orders to be placed during the year is:

options.A: 30 orders
options.B: 24 orders
options.C: 20 orders
options.D: 40 orders

e: Number of orders = annual demand / EOQ = 24,000 / 800 = 30 orders per year.

q: The annual demand for a material is 36,000 units and its Economic Order Quantity is 1,200 units, reckoning a year of 360 days. The time interval between two successive orders is:

options.A: 10 days
options.B: 30 days
options.C: 12 days
options.D: 15 days

e: Orders per year = 36,000 / 1,200 = 30. Interval between orders = 360 / 30 = 12 days.

q: An enterprise proposes to extend its credit period. The extension is expected to raise sales by Rs 10,00,000, on which the contribution margin is 20 per cent. The average receivables will rise by Rs 3,00,000, the cost of capital is 15 per cent, and additional bad debts are estimated at 1 per cent of the incremental sales. The net benefit of the proposal is:
e: Net benefit = incremental contribution Rs 2,00,000 - cost of capital 15% x Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 45,000 - bad debts 1% x Rs 10,00,000 = Rs 10,000, i.e. Rs 1,45,000.

q: A supplier offers terms of 3/10, net 45, that is, a discount of 3 per cent for payment within 10 days and the full amount payable in 45 days. The approximate annualised cost of foregoing the discount, reckoning a year of 365 days, is about:

options.A: 12.1 per cent
options.B: 32.3 per cent
options.C: 24.3 per cent
options.D: 3.1 per cent

e: Cost of foregoing discount = [3/(100-3)] x [365/(45-10)] = 3.09% x 10.43 = about 32.3% per annum.

q: Factoring of receivables differs from ordinary bill discounting mainly in that the factor, besides financing the receivables, also:

options.A: Undertakes services such as sales-ledger administration and collection of the debts, and in non-recourse factoring bears the loss from bad debts
options.B: Lends only against the security of immovable property of the enterprise
options.C: Requires the enterprise to repay the advance even before the customer pays, in every type of factoring
options.D: Is confined to the discounting of bills of exchange drawn on the government alone

e: Besides financing receivables, a factor provides sales-ledger administration and collection services, and in non-recourse factoring bears bad-debt losses.

q: A lock-box system is adopted by an enterprise for collecting its receivables primarily in order to:

options.A: Increase the credit period allowed to its customers
options.B: Postpone payment to its own suppliers for a longer period
options.C: Avoid maintaining any bank account for collections
options.D: Reduce the collection (mail and processing) float, by having customers remit to local post-office boxes from where the bank collects and credits the proceeds quickly

e: A lock-box has customers remit to local post-office boxes cleared quickly by the bank, cutting mail and processing float and speeding collection.

q: Trade credit and accrued wages and expenses are described as spontaneous sources of working capital finance because they:

options.A: Are available only after a formal loan agreement with a bank is executed
options.B: Carry the highest rate of interest among all sources of finance
options.C: Arise automatically, in the ordinary course of business, roughly in step with the level of operations, without a separate financing decision
options.D: Are raised from the shareholders of the enterprise

e: Trade credit and accrued expenses arise automatically in ordinary operations, roughly with the level of activity, without a separate financing decision, hence spontaneous.

q: An enterprise disburses Rs 2,00,000 per day. By changing its disbursement arrangements it increases its disbursement float by 3 days, without delaying any payment beyond its due date. The amount of funds so released for use is:
e: Funds released = daily disbursement x extra float days = Rs 2,00,000 x 3 = Rs 6,00,000.

q: Under the Baumol model, the optimum cash balance of an enterprise at each conversion is Rs 60,000. Assuming the balance is spent evenly and replenished at that level, its average cash balance is:
e: Under Baumol, cash falls evenly from Rs 60,000 to zero, so average balance = Rs 60,000 / 2 = Rs 30,000.

q: An enterprise needs Rs 18,00,000 in cash during a year and its optimum cash balance per conversion under the Baumol model is Rs 60,000. The number of conversions of securities into cash it will make during the year is:

options.A: 30 conversions
options.B: 18 conversions
options.C: 60 conversions
options.D: 12 conversions

e: Number of conversions = total annual cash need / optimum balance = Rs 18,00,000 / Rs 60,000 = 30 conversions.

q: Which of the following is a spontaneous source of working capital finance?

options.A: A term loan raised from a financial institution
options.B: A fresh issue of equity shares
options.C: Credit allowed by suppliers of raw material in the ordinary course of purchases
options.D: A debenture issue made to the public

e: Supplier credit for raw material arises spontaneously in ordinary purchases, unlike term loans, shares or debentures which need formal raising.

q: Commercial paper, as a source of short-term finance for working capital, can be issued only by:

options.A: Any partnership firm, however small, without any condition
options.B: Creditworthy companies satisfying the prescribed eligibility conditions such as minimum net worth and a credit rating, for raising funds directly from investors for a short maturity
options.C: Enterprises which have defaulted on their bank borrowings
options.D: Co-operative societies alone

e: Commercial paper can be issued only by creditworthy companies meeting prescribed eligibility conditions like minimum net worth and a credit rating, for short maturities.

q: An enterprise whose sales are expanding very fast shows a falling current ratio, lengthening overdrafts and increasing dependence on supplier credit, even though it reports profits. These are typical symptoms of:

options.A: Under-trading, that is, carrying far more working capital than its operations need
options.B: A permanent surplus of long-term funds in the business
options.C: Complete absence of any credit sales
options.D: Over-trading, that is, expanding operations beyond what its working capital can support

e: Rapid expansion outrunning working capital, with falling current ratio and stretched overdrafts and supplier credit despite profits, is over-trading.

q: Working capital leverage refers to the effect on the return on capital employed when:

options.A: The investment in current assets is reduced while sales and operating profit are maintained, so that the same profit is earned on a smaller capital base, though with greater liquidity risk
options.B: The proportion of debt in the capital structure is increased, whatever happens to current assets
options.C: Fixed assets are replaced by current assets of the same value
options.D: The credit period allowed to customers is lengthened without any change in sales

e: Working capital leverage is earning the same operating profit on a smaller current-asset base, raising return on capital employed though with greater liquidity risk.

q: The daily operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 25,000. Its operating cycle lengthens by 10 days, other things remaining the same. The additional working capital it will require is:
e: Additional working capital = daily operating cost x extra cycle days = Rs 25,000 x 10 = Rs 2,50,000.

q: The projected sales of an enterprise for the coming year are Rs 84,00,000 and, on the percentage-of-sales method, its working capital is estimated at 15 per cent of sales. The working capital required by the enterprise is:
e: Working capital = 15% of projected sales = 15% x Rs 84,00,000 = Rs 12,60,000.

q: The working capital of an enterprise is estimated from the following components: raw material stock Rs 2,40,000, work-in-progress Rs 1,20,000, finished goods stock Rs 3,00,000, debtors Rs 4,20,000 and cash Rs 60,000; against these, trade creditors are Rs 1,80,000 and outstanding wages are Rs 40,000. The net working capital required is:
e: Current assets total Rs 11,40,000; current liabilities Rs 1,80,000 + Rs 40,000 = Rs 2,20,000. Net working capital = Rs 11,40,000 - Rs 2,20,000 = Rs 9,20,000.

q: The net working capital of an enterprise is estimated at Rs 12,50,000. A margin of 8 per cent is added for contingencies. The total working capital to be provided for is:
e: Total working capital = Rs 12,50,000 + 8% contingency = Rs 12,50,000 x 1.08 = Rs 13,50,000.

q: A cold-storage enterprise needs heavy funds for a few months of the year to buy and store the seasonal produce, while for the rest of the year its requirement is small and steady. The heavy seasonal requirement is an example of:

options.A: Fluctuating (temporary) working capital, over and above the permanent minimum level maintained throughout the year
options.B: Permanent (core) working capital, because it recurs every year
options.C: Fixed capital, because the produce is stored in its own building
options.D: Gross working capital of the enterprise as a whole

e: A heavy need for only a few months, above the steady year-round minimum, is fluctuating or temporary working capital, not permanent core capital.

q: VED analysis, used for the control of spare-parts inventory, classifies items as Vital, Essential and Desirable primarily on the basis of:

options.A: The annual consumption value of the items
options.B: The criticality of the item for production, that is, the seriousness of the stoppage or loss caused if the item is not available when needed
options.C: The physical size and weight of the items
options.D: The speed with which the items move out of the stores

e: VED analysis classifies spares as Vital, Essential and Desirable by criticality, i.e. the seriousness of stoppage if the item is unavailable when needed.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 18,25,000 and its average inventory during the year is Rs 2,50,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. The number of days for which inventory is held, on an average, is:

options.A: 7.3 days
options.B: 73 days
options.C: 36.5 days
options.D: 50 days

e: Inventory turnover = Rs 18,25,000 / Rs 2,50,000 = 7.3 times. Days held = 365 / 7.3 = 50 days.

q: The debtors of an enterprise stand at Rs 4,00,000 and its annual credit sales are Rs 36,50,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. Its average collection period is:

options.A: 30 days
options.B: 36.5 days
options.C: 40 days
options.D: 45 days

e: Average collection period = (Rs 4,00,000 / Rs 36,50,000) x 365 = 40 days.

q: A division keeps its profit unchanged but increases the sales generated from the same capital employed. In Du Pont terms, the resulting rise in its Return on Investment comes through an improvement in:

options.A: The profit margin on sales alone
options.B: The capital turnover ratio
options.C: The capital charge rate
options.D: The residual income of the division

e: In Du Pont terms ROI = margin x capital turnover; with profit unchanged, more sales from the same capital raises ROI through higher capital turnover.

q: A division earns a controllable profit of Rs 5,40,000 on capital employed of Rs 36,00,000. Its Return on Investment is:

A divisional manager judged on Residual Income is more likely than one judged on Return on Investment to accept a new project whose return exceeds the enterprise's cost of capital but is below the division's present ROI, because:

options.A: Residual Income rises whenever a project earns more than the capital charge on the investment it requires
options.B: Residual Income is expressed as a percentage and therefore always rises with new investment
options.C: Residual Income ignores the capital employed in the division altogether
options.D: Residual Income is computed before charging any cost of capital

e: Residual Income rises for any project earning above the capital charge, so an RI-judged manager accepts it even if it dilutes the division's percentage ROI.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 3,10,000 on capital employed of Rs 31,00,000. The required rate of return is 12 per cent. Its Residual Income is:

options.B: Nil

q: Economic Value Added is best described as the value created in a period after meeting:

options.A: Only the interest payable to lenders
options.B: The cost of all capital employed, both debt and equity, applied to the net operating profit after tax
options.C: Only the dividend expected by equity shareholders
options.D: The depreciation charge on the assets employed

e: EVA is value created after meeting the cost of all capital, debt and equity, charged on capital employed against net operating profit after tax.

q: The Net Operating Profit After Tax of a division is Rs 9,60,000, its capital employed is Rs 60,00,000 and the weighted average cost of capital is 11 per cent. Its Economic Value Added is:

A division disposes of a long-idle asset that was earning nothing, its operating profit remaining the same and the sale proceeds being returned to head office. Other things equal, the disposal will improve its Economic Value Added mainly because:

options.A: Its sales turnover necessarily rises
options.B: Its tax charge for the year falls to nil
options.C: The capital on which the capital charge is levied becomes smaller
options.D: Its weighted average cost of capital becomes zero

e: Disposing of an idle asset reduces capital employed, so the capital charge falls and EVA improves while operating profit stays the same.

q: A supplying division is working at full capacity and must turn away outside customers to meet an internal order. For goal congruence, the minimum transfer price it should charge must cover:

options.A: Its fixed cost per unit only
options.B: The historical cost recorded in its books
options.C: Only the depreciation on the plant used
options.D: Its variable cost per unit plus the contribution lost on the outside sales displaced

e: At full capacity, the minimum transfer price must cover variable cost plus the contribution lost on outside sales displaced by the internal order.

q: A supplying division has a variable cost of Rs 82 per unit. It works at full capacity and loses a contribution of Rs 28 per unit on outside sales for every unit transferred internally. The minimum transfer price per unit it should accept is:

options.A: Rs 82
options.B: Rs 110
options.C: Rs 54
options.D: Rs 138

e: Minimum transfer price = variable cost Rs 82 + lost contribution Rs 28 = Rs 110 per unit.

q: The full cost of a component in the supplying division is Rs 240 per unit. Transfers are priced at full cost plus a mark-up of 25 per cent on cost. The transfer price per unit is:

options.A: Rs 265
options.B: Rs 288
options.C: Rs 300
options.D: Rs 320

e: Transfer price = full cost Rs 240 + 25% mark-up Rs 60 = Rs 300 per unit.

q: The outside market price of an intermediate product is Rs 175 per unit. On an internal transfer, selling and distribution expenses of Rs 10 per unit that are incurred on outside sales are saved. The adjusted market-based transfer price per unit is:

options.A: Rs 165
options.B: Rs 175
options.C: Rs 185
options.D: Rs 160

e: Adjusted market price = outside market price Rs 175 - selling expenses saved Rs 10 = Rs 165 per unit.

q: Negotiated transfer prices can work satisfactorily only where:

options.A: Head office fixes both the price and the quantity in every case
options.B: The buying division is compelled to buy internally at any price named
options.C: The supplying division has no knowledge of its own costs
options.D: Both divisions enjoy autonomy, have access to cost and market information, and are free to deal outside if terms are not agreed

e: Negotiated pricing works only with divisional autonomy, access to cost and market information, and freedom to buy or sell outside if terms are not agreed.

q: Under dual pricing of inter-divisional transfers, the supplying division is credited at one price and the buying division is charged at a different price. A direct consequence for performance measurement is that:

options.A: The sum of the divisional profits exceeds the profit of the enterprise as a whole, the difference being eliminated on consolidation
options.B: The profit of the enterprise as a whole can never be ascertained
options.C: Both divisions necessarily show a loss on the transfer
options.D: The transfer has no effect on the profit of either division

e: Under dual pricing the two divisions use different prices, so summed divisional profits exceed company profit, the difference being eliminated on consolidation.

q: Goal congruence in a divisionalised enterprise means that:

options.A: A manager pursuing the goals set for his own division, as measured by his performance indicators, also acts in the best interests of the enterprise as a whole
options.B: All divisions earn exactly the same rate of return
options.C: Head office takes every operating decision for the divisions
options.D: Divisions are prevented from dealing with one another

e: Goal congruence means a manager pursuing his divisional goals, as measured by his indicators, also acts in the best interests of the enterprise as a whole.

q: A divisional manager rejects a sound expansion only because accepting it would dilute the high percentage ROI by which he is judged, even though the expansion earns well above the cost of capital. This behaviour is a recognised dysfunction of:

options.A: Residual Income as a performance measure
options.B: Market-based transfer pricing
options.C: Return on Investment as a performance measure
options.D: Negotiated transfer pricing

e: Rejecting a sound project to protect a high percentage ROI, even though it earns above cost of capital, is a recognised dysfunction of ROI measurement.

q: A proposed project requires an investment of Rs 10,00,000 and is expected to earn a profit of Rs 1,60,000 a year. The cost of capital is 12 per cent. The annual Residual Income expected from the project is:
In a Balanced Scorecard, measures such as the percentage of sales from new products and the customer retention rate are valued chiefly because, unlike the period's profit, they act as:

options.A: Statutory disclosures in the annual accounts
options.B: Purely historical records of past results
options.C: Measures that need no target to be set for them
options.D: Leading indicators that signal future financial performance

e: Measures like sales from new products and customer retention are leading indicators signalling future financial performance, unlike current profit which records the past.

q: For a manufacturing division applying the Balanced Scorecard, the measure that fits the internal business process perspective most appropriately is:

options.A: The defect and rework rate in production
options.B: The return on capital employed of the division
options.C: The market share of the division's products
options.D: The hours of training provided per employee

e: Defect and rework rate measures production process performance, so it belongs to the internal business process perspective of the Balanced Scorecard.

q: For a division applying the Balanced Scorecard, expenditure on upgrading employees' skills and improving its information systems belongs primarily to the:

options.A: Financial perspective
options.B: Customer perspective
options.C: Learning and growth perspective
options.D: Internal business process perspective

e: Upgrading employee skills and information systems builds capability for the future, so it belongs to the learning and growth perspective.

q: A strategy map in the Balanced Scorecard is used to:

options.A: Replace the annual budget of the enterprise
options.B: Show, in cause-and-effect form, how objectives under the several perspectives are linked and together deliver the strategy
options.C: Record the actual cost of each product manufactured
options.D: Fix the transfer prices between divisions

e: A strategy map shows in cause-and-effect form how objectives under the several perspectives link together to deliver the strategy.

q: A scorecard that merely collects a long list of unrelated financial and non-financial measures, without linking them to the strategy of the enterprise, fails as a Balanced Scorecard mainly because:

options.A: It contains too few financial measures
options.B: It is prepared more than once a year
options.C: It uses non-financial measures at all
options.D: Balance requires the measures to be tied together by the strategy and by cause-and-effect relationships, not simply assembled

e: A Balanced Scorecard fails if measures are merely assembled; balance requires them tied together by strategy and cause-and-effect relationships.

q: Non-financial measures of performance are brought into performance evaluation along with financial measures mainly because financial measures alone:

options.A: Report results after the event and reveal little about how the result was achieved or what is being built for the future
options.B: Are expressed in money terms
options.C: Are prepared by the accounts department
options.D: Cannot be compared from one year to another

e: Financial measures alone report results after the event and reveal little about how they were achieved or what is being built for the future, hence non-financial measures are added.

q: A division compares the working of one of its own functions, such as its stores or payroll function, with the same function in an enterprise in a different industry that performs it exceptionally well. This is an example of:

options.A: Internal benchmarking
options.B: Competitive benchmarking
options.C: Functional benchmarking
options.D: Product benchmarking only

e: Comparing a function like stores or payroll with the same function in a different industry that performs it exceptionally well is functional benchmarking.

q: In a benchmarking exercise, the step that must come before practices are adapted from the benchmark partner is:

options.A: Publishing the division's own results
options.B: Measuring the performance gap and understanding the practices and conditions that produce the partner's superior performance
options.C: Changing the name of the process studied
options.D: Fixing the next year's budget allotment

e: Before adapting a partner's practices, the performance gap must be measured and the practices and conditions producing superior performance understood.

q: Under Total Quality Management, spending more on the prevention of defects is expected, over time, to:

options.A: Increase the cost of inspection and of failures by the same amount
options.B: Make inspection of the finished output unnecessary in every case at once
options.C: Raise the total cost of quality permanently
options.D: Reduce the appraisal and failure costs by more than the extra prevention cost, so that the total cost of quality falls

e: Under TQM, extra prevention spending reduces appraisal and failure costs by more than the extra cost, so total cost of quality falls over time.

q: Total Quality Management, as an approach to performance improvement, rests most fundamentally on:

options.A: Continuous improvement involving all employees, with the requirements of the customer as the focus of quality
options.B: Inspection of every unit of output at the final stage alone
options.C: Punishing the worker responsible for every defect found
options.D: Producing strictly to the minimum specification at the lowest cost

e: TQM rests fundamentally on continuous improvement involving all employees, with customer requirements as the focus of quality.

q: A divisional performance report that is to be used for judging the divisional manager should present the result of the division most usefully by:

options.A: Charging all head-office costs to the division without identifying them separately
options.B: Showing only the final profit after every allocation made by head office
options.C: Separating the controllable profit of the division from items beyond the manager's control, which are shown distinctly
options.D: Omitting all fixed costs of the division

e: A report for judging the manager should separate controllable profit from items beyond his control, shown distinctly, rather than burying them in allocations.

q: The level of detail in a performance report should be graded by the level of management receiving it, so that a report for top management is characteristically:

options.A: A listing of every transaction of the period
options.B: A summarised report highlighting the significant results, trends and exceptions across the divisions
options.C: Confined to the cash transactions of one section
options.D: Identical in content to the report sent to a foreman

e: Detail is graded by management level, so top management gets a summarised report highlighting significant results, trends and exceptions across divisions.

q: Divisional autonomy in performance evaluation is undermined most directly when:

options.A: A divisional manager is consulted before his targets are set
options.B: Divisions are allowed to choose between internal transfer and outside purchase
options.C: Performance reports are sent to the divisional manager regularly
options.D: Head office routinely overrules the divisional manager's operating decisions yet continues to judge him on the division's profit

e: Autonomy is undermined when head office routinely overrules the manager's operating decisions yet still judges him on divisional profit.

q: The arm's length principle, applied to transfer pricing, requires that the price charged on a transfer between two units be:

options.A: The price that would have been charged on a comparable transaction between independent parties dealing at arm's length
options.B: Always the variable cost of the supplying unit
options.C: Fixed once for all years by head office
options.D: Lower than any price charged to an outside customer

e: The arm's length principle requires the transfer price to be what independent parties would charge on a comparable transaction at arm's length.

q: The Return on Investment of a division using old plant written down to a low book value tends to appear flattering in comparison with a division using new plant, mainly because:

options.A: The old plant necessarily produces better quality output
options.B: The sales of the old-plant division are always higher
options.C: Its profit is necessarily free of all depreciation
options.D: The capital employed in its denominator is low, so the same profit yields a higher percentage return

e: Old plant at low book value gives a low capital-employed denominator, so the same profit yields a flattering higher percentage ROI.

q: A division has sales of Rs 96,00,000, a profit of Rs 7,20,000 and capital employed of Rs 48,00,000. Its Return on Investment, worked out as profit margin multiplied by capital turnover, is:

A division earns a profit before interest and tax of Rs 14,00,000. The tax rate is 25 per cent, its capital employed is Rs 70,00,000 and the weighted average cost of capital is 10 per cent. Its Economic Value Added is:

A supplying division with spare capacity has a variable cost of Rs 90 per unit and no lost outside contribution. The buying division can purchase the same article outside at Rs 135 per unit. The range within which a negotiated transfer price per unit can settle to the benefit of both divisions is:

options.A: Between Rs 90 and Rs 135
options.B: Between Rs 135 and Rs 160
options.C: Between Rs 45 and Rs 90
options.D: Exactly Rs 135 in all cases

e: With spare capacity the floor is variable cost Rs 90 and the ceiling is the buyer's outside price Rs 135, so a mutually beneficial price lies between Rs 90 and Rs 135.

q: Division A earns a profit of Rs 8,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 50,00,000, and Division B earns a profit of Rs 4,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 20,00,000. The required rate of return is 10 per cent for both. Judged by Residual Income:

options.A: Division B is better, with Rs 3,00,000 against Rs 2,00,000 of Division A
options.B: Both divisions have the same Residual Income
options.C: Division A is better, with Rs 3,00,000 against Rs 2,00,000 of Division B
options.D: Neither division earns any Residual Income

q: The controllable Return on Investment of a division is computed by relating:

options.A: The profit after all head-office allocations to the total assets of the enterprise
options.B: The controllable profit of the division to the capital employed that is controllable by the divisional manager
options.C: The sales of the division to its variable costs
options.D: The residual income of the division to its sales

e: Controllable ROI relates the division's controllable profit to the capital employed controllable by the divisional manager.

q: Under the two-part tariff method of transfer pricing, the buying division is charged:

options.A: Only a single price equal to the market price for every unit
options.B: Only a fixed annual fee, with nothing for the units actually transferred
options.C: The full cost of the supplying division plus a mark-up on every unit
options.D: A variable charge per unit transferred, broadly at variable cost, plus a fixed periodic fee towards the fixed costs and profit of the supplying division

e: Under two-part tariff, the buyer pays a variable charge per unit, broadly at variable cost, plus a fixed periodic fee towards the supplier's fixed costs and profit.

q: Where there is no outside market at all for an intermediate product transferred between divisions, the transfer price is most commonly based on:

options.A: Cost, with or without a mark-up, or on negotiation founded on cost information
options.B: The price of the final product sold to customers
options.C: The price charged for a wholly different product that has a market
options.D: A price fixed by the external auditors of the enterprise

e: With no outside market for an intermediate product, transfer price is most commonly based on cost, with or without mark-up, or negotiation founded on cost.

q: A division reports, along with its monthly profit, the number of customer complaints received and the proportion of deliveries made on time. In performance evaluation these two measures are useful chiefly as:

options.A: Substitutes for the profit figure in the annual accounts
options.B: Measures that can be expressed only in money terms
options.C: Non-financial indicators of service quality that help explain present results and foreshadow future results
options.D: Items to be reported only after the close of the financial year

e: Complaints and on-time delivery are non-financial indicators of service quality that help explain present results and foreshadow future results.

q: A divisional manager who expects that a good performance this year will simply be met by a proportionately harder target next year may hold back performance in the current year. This behaviour in target setting is known as the:

options.A: Controllability effect
options.B: Ratchet effect
options.C: Learning curve effect
options.D: Leverage effect

e: Holding back performance because good results bring harder targets next year is the ratchet effect in target setting.

q: Economic Value Added differs from the Residual Income of a division most essentially in that Economic Value Added:

options.A: Makes no charge at all for the capital employed
options.B: Is always expressed as a percentage of sales
options.C: Ignores the tax charge on operating profit
options.D: Is built on the net operating profit after tax and the weighted average cost of capital, with adjustments to accounting profit and capital to reflect economic value

e: EVA is built on net operating profit after tax and weighted average cost of capital, with adjustments to accounting profit and capital to reflect economic value.

q: For a service division applying the Balanced Scorecard, the measure that fits the customer perspective most appropriately is:

options.A: The cost per transaction processed by the division
options.B: The percentage of employees who completed refresher training
options.C: The proportion of service requests completed within the promised time
options.D: The return on the assets used by the division

e: For a service division, the proportion of requests completed within promised time measures service to customers, fitting the customer perspective.

q: A division adopts, without change, the practices of a benchmark partner operating on a much larger scale and under different conditions, and the expected gains do not materialise. The failure illustrates that benchmarking:

options.A: Can be applied only within the same industry
options.B: Requires the practices found to be adapted to the division's own scale, conditions and capabilities before they are introduced
options.C: Is of no use for improving any process
options.D: Must always be kept secret from the employees concerned

e: Benchmarking fails when practices are copied unchanged; they must be adapted to the division's own scale, conditions and capabilities before introduction.

q: In a Total Quality Management programme, quality circles contribute to performance improvement mainly by:

options.A: Inspecting the output of other departments and reporting defects to management
options.B: Fixing the quality standards for the whole enterprise
options.C: Bringing together small groups of employees doing similar work to identify, analyse and solve quality problems in their own area
options.D: Replacing the formal training of employees altogether

e: Quality circles bring together small groups doing similar work to identify, analyse and solve quality problems in their own area.

q: A modern divisional performance report best serves evaluation and control when, besides the budgeted and actual financial results and the variances on them, it also sets out:

options.A: Only the transactions that were posted after the close of the period
options.B: The names of the officers who prepared the report
options.C: A repetition of the budget figures of the previous year without comment
options.D: The significant non-financial indicators of the division and the explanations of major variances with the corrective action proposed

e: A modern report best serves control when, besides budgeted and actual results and variances, it gives key non-financial indicators and explanations with corrective action.

q: In process costing, when an abnormal gain arises, the scrap value that would have been realised on the units of normal loss so saved is dealt with by:

options.A: Crediting it to the process account as an additional output of the process
options.B: Debiting it to the Abnormal Gain Account, so that only the net gain is ultimately transferred to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.C: Ignoring it altogether, since no scrap is actually produced on those units
options.D: Crediting it to the general Profit and Loss Account as a miscellaneous receipt

e: On abnormal gain, the scrap value of normal-loss units saved is debited to the Abnormal Gain Account, so only the net gain reaches the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: Under the FIFO method of valuing work-in-progress in process costing, the equivalent units of a period are computed by:

options.A: Counting only the work done in the current period, the work done on the opening work-in-progress in the previous period being excluded
options.B: Counting the whole of the opening work-in-progress again as work of the current period
options.C: Adding the opening and closing work-in-progress together without any adjustment for the stage of completion
options.D: Treating every partly complete unit in stock as a fully complete unit

e: Under FIFO, equivalent units count only work done in the current period; work already done on opening WIP in the previous period is excluded.

q: Co-products are distinguished from joint products in that co-products:

options.A: Are always of negligible value in relation to the main product
options.B: Can never be sold without further processing after they arise
options.C: Are produced from different raw materials or by different processes and do not arise from a common input at a split-off point
options.D: Are produced wholly by accident and are never planned in advance

e: Co-products are produced from different raw materials or processes and do not arise from a common input at a split-off point, unlike joint products.

q: Under the standard cost method of accounting for a by-product, the by-product is:

options.A: Credited to the process account at its actual sale proceeds of the period, whatever they may be
options.B: Charged with the whole joint cost of the process in which it arises
options.C: Never recorded in the cost accounts until the whole of it has been sold
options.D: Valued at a predetermined standard cost per unit, and that standard value is credited to the joint process account

e: Under the standard cost method, the by-product is valued at a predetermined standard cost per unit and that standard value is credited to the joint process account.

q: In a process, the opening work-in-progress is 600 units, 50% complete in respect of all cost elements. During the period, 7,000 units are completed and transferred to the next process, and the closing work-in-progress is 1,000 units, 60% complete in respect of all cost elements. On the FIFO basis, the equivalent production for the period is:

options.A: 7,900 units
options.B: 7,600 units
options.C: 7,300 units
options.D: 7,000 units

e: FIFO equivalent units = completed 7,000 + closing WIP 1,000 x 60% - opening WIP 600 x 50% = 7,000 + 600 - 300 = 7,300 units.

q: Where processes transfer their output to one another at a price loaded with profit, the closing stock of a process is shown in the balance sheet of the factory at:

options.A: The actual cost of production to the factory as a whole, excluding any element of inter-process profit
options.B: The transfer price at which it was received from the earlier process
options.C: The market price at which it could be sold outside the factory
options.D: Nil, until the finished product made out of it is sold

e: Closing stock is shown in the balance sheet at actual cost to the factory as a whole, excluding any inter-process profit loaded in transfer prices.

q: A tonne-kilometre, used as the cost unit in the operating costing of a goods transport undertaking, is called a composite cost unit because it:

options.A: Is made up of the costs of several vehicles added together
options.B: Combines two measures into one unit, namely the weight carried and the distance over which it is carried
options.C: Includes both the standing charges and the running charges of the undertaking
options.D: Is compiled jointly by the accounts department and the traffic department

e: A tonne-kilometre is a composite cost unit because it combines two measures, the weight carried and the distance over which it is carried.

q: Under the integral (integrated) system of accounting, cost and financial transactions are recorded:

options.A: In two entirely separate sets of books which are reconciled at the end of the year
options.B: Only in the cost ledger, the financial books being dispensed with altogether
options.C: Only in memorandum registers maintained outside the double-entry system
options.D: In one single set of books, so that no separate Cost Ledger Adjustment Account and no reconciliation of the two profits are needed

e: Under integral accounting, cost and financial transactions are recorded in one single set of books, so no Cost Ledger Adjustment Account or reconciliation is needed.

q: In a process, 8,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 3,06,400. Normal loss is 5% of the input and the scrap realises Rs 6 per unit. The actual output obtained is 7,350 units. The value of the abnormal loss is:
e: Expected output = 8,000 - 400 = 7,600; abnormal loss = 250 units. Cost per unit = (Rs 3,06,400 - 400 x Rs 6) / 7,600 = Rs 40. Abnormal loss = 250 x Rs 40 = Rs 10,000.

q: Under the contribution method of apportioning joint costs, the joint cost is apportioned among the joint products in the ratio of:

options.A: The physical quantities of output of the several products
options.B: The number of workers employed on each product after the split-off point
options.C: The contribution earned by each product, that is, its sales value less the variable and separable costs incurred on it after the split-off point
options.D: The factory overheads absorbed by each product during the period

e: Under the contribution method, joint cost is apportioned in the ratio of contribution, i.e. sales value less variable and separable costs after split-off.

q: In a reconciliation of cost and financial accounts which starts with the profit as per the financial accounts, interest on capital charged only in the cost accounts is:

options.A: Deducted from the financial profit, because the cost profit is lower by that amount
options.B: Added to the financial profit, because it is an income of the business
options.C: Ignored, because notional charges never affect a reconciliation
options.D: Shown only as a memorandum note below the reconciliation statement

e: Starting from financial profit, notional interest on capital charged only in cost accounts is deducted, because cost profit is lower by that amount.

q: In the operating costing of a road transport undertaking, which of the following is a maintenance charge?

options.A: The annual road licence fee of the vehicle
options.B: The salary of the traffic manager of the undertaking
options.C: The diesel and lubricating oil consumed in running the vehicle
options.D: Repairs, overhauls and servicing of the vehicles

e: Repairs, overhauls and servicing of vehicles are maintenance charges; licence is a standing charge and diesel a running charge in operating costing.

q: In a process, 12,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 4,94,400. Normal loss is 10% of the input and the scrap realises Rs 7 per unit. The cost per unit of the good output is:

options.A: Rs 45
options.C: Rs 48
options.D: Rs 38

q: In contract costing, plant which was issued to a contract site and is returned to the stores before the completion of the contract is dealt with by:

options.A: Crediting the Contract Account with its original cost, ignoring the wear and tear at the site
options.B: Crediting the Contract Account with its written-down value, that is, its value after providing for depreciation for the period it remained at the site
options.C: Debiting the Contract Account again with its full replacement price
options.D: Writing it off entirely to the Costing Profit and Loss Account as a loss

e: Plant returned to stores is credited to the Contract Account at written-down value, i.e. after depreciation for the period it remained at the site.

q: The Abnormal Loss Account opened in process costing is finally closed by:

options.A: Crediting the whole value of the abnormal loss to the process account of the next process
options.B: Carrying its balance forward indefinitely as an asset of the factory
options.C: Crediting it with the scrap actually realised on the abnormal loss units and transferring the balance, being the net loss, to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.D: Debiting it with the scrap value of the normal loss of the process

e: The Abnormal Loss Account is credited with scrap actually realised on abnormal loss units, and its balance, the net loss, is transferred to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: Under the constant gross margin method of apportioning joint costs, the share of joint cost borne by a joint product is arrived at by:

options.A: Apportioning the joint cost in the ratio of the weights of the products at the split-off point
options.B: Deducting from the final sales value of the product an amount of gross margin computed at a uniform overall percentage, and then deducting its separable costs after the split-off point
options.C: Charging the joint cost wholly to the product which has the highest final sales value
options.D: Dividing the joint cost equally among all the joint products, whatever their sales values

e: Under constant gross margin, deduct from final sales value a gross margin at a uniform overall percentage, then deduct separable costs, to get the joint cost share.

q: A joint cost of Rs 7,20,000 is to be apportioned among joint products X, Y and Z on the physical units basis. The outputs are: X — 3,000 kg, Y — 2,000 kg and Z — 1,000 kg. The share of joint cost borne by product Y is:
The replacement cost method of accounting for a by-product is applied where the by-product is:

options.A: Used within the factory itself in place of a material that would otherwise have to be purchased, and it is credited to the process at the cost of the material it replaces
options.B: Sold in the open market at the highest price obtainable during the year
options.C: Destroyed immediately after it arises, having no use or value at all
options.D: Further processed into the main product of a subsequent process

e: The replacement cost method applies where the by-product is used inside the factory in place of a purchased material and is credited at the cost of material replaced.

q: Under the non-integral (interlocking) system, the account maintained in the financial books to summarise the transactions recorded in the cost ledger is the:

options.A: Work-in-Progress Ledger Control Account
options.B: Stores Ledger Control Account
options.C: Cost Ledger Control Account
options.D: Costing Profit and Loss Account

e: Under the non-integral system, the Cost Ledger Control Account in the financial books summarises transactions recorded in the cost ledger.

q: Which of the following items appears in the financial accounts of an enterprise but is not recorded in its cost accounts?

options.A: Wages paid to the direct workers engaged on production
options.B: Interest and dividends received on investments held by the enterprise
options.C: Depreciation charged on the factory plant and machinery
options.D: Cost of the stores consumed in the factory during the period

e: Interest and dividends received on investments are financial-account items only; they are not recorded in cost accounts, unlike wages, depreciation and stores.

q: A joint cost of Rs 6,00,000 is to be apportioned between joint products A and B by the net realisable value method. A can be sold for Rs 8,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 2,00,000. B can be sold for Rs 5,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 1,00,000. The share of joint cost borne by product A is:
A recognised difficulty in applying the market value (sales value at split-off) method of apportioning joint costs is that:

options.A: It requires the physical output of each product to be weighed at the split-off point
options.B: It can be used only where all the joint products are sold without any further processing
options.C: It charges no joint cost at all to the product having the lowest sales value
options.D: Market prices at the split-off point may not exist for products which are never sold in that intermediate state

e: Market value at split-off may not exist for products never sold in that intermediate state, a recognised difficulty of the sales value method.

q: In a process, all the material is introduced at the very beginning of the process. The closing work-in-progress of the process will accordingly be taken, for the purpose of equivalent units in respect of material cost, as:

options.A: Nil, because the units are not yet complete
options.B: Complete only to the same extent as it is complete in respect of labour cost
options.C: Fully complete, that is, at 100 per cent of its units
options.D: Complete to one-half of its units in every case

e: Material introduced at the start is fully in closing WIP, so for material cost the closing WIP counts as 100% complete for equivalent units.

q: A joint product can be sold at the split-off point for Rs 48 per unit. It can alternatively be processed further at an additional cost of Rs 17 per unit and then sold for Rs 72 per unit. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Sell it at the split-off point, because the joint cost has already been incurred on it
options.B: Process it further, because the additional revenue of Rs 24 per unit exceeds the additional cost of Rs 17 per unit by Rs 7 per unit
options.C: Process it further only if the whole of the joint cost apportioned to it is also recovered
options.D: Stop producing the product altogether, since further processing always adds to cost

e: Further processing adds revenue Rs 72 - Rs 48 = Rs 24 against added cost Rs 17, a gain of Rs 7 per unit, so processing further is correct; joint cost is sunk.

q: In the operating costing of a staff canteen run by an enterprise, the most appropriate cost unit for expressing the cost of the service is the cost:

options.A: Per meal served by the canteen
options.B: Per kilogram of provisions purchased for the canteen
options.C: Per employee on the rolls of the enterprise
options.D: Per day for which the canteen building remains open

e: For a staff canteen, the appropriate service cost unit is cost per meal served, reflecting the output of the service.
